Chapter 3: Pop Culture’s Role in Reinforcing and Challenging Norms
Let’s talk about something that’s all around us, even when we’re not really paying attention—pop culture.
From the moment you’re a kid, you’re surrounded by stories. Whether it’s on TV, in your favorite movies, through music, or scrolling online, these stories are more than just entertainment. They’re little lessons about what’s normal, what’s funny, and what’s even possible.
Have you ever noticed how these stories teach us who gets to be the hero, who’s usually the punchline, or who barely even shows up? It’s almost like they’re quietly setting the rules for what’s valued—and what’s not.
Picture a teenager curled up on the couch, watching their favorite sitcom. The jokes fly by, the characters feel like old friends, and everything seems safe and familiar. But, if you look a little closer, you’ll see patterns hiding under the laughs. Women are often there just to support the men, jokes about race or gender get shrugged off, and anyone who doesn’t fit the usual mold? They’re either a problem to solve, or just the butt of the joke.
These patterns are easy to miss, especially when they’re wrapped in nostalgia. We remember the shows and movies we loved as kids, and honestly, it can feel pretty uncomfortable to admit that some of those stories weren’t so harmless after all. When someone points this out, the reaction is often, “It’s just a joke! Don’t ruin it for me.” Sound familiar?
But here’s something important—pop culture isn’t neutral. The stories we watch and listen to actually shape the way we see ourselves and the people around us. When the same types of characters always get to be the heroes, and others are stuck as sidekicks or villains, it really sends a message about who matters and who doesn’t. And when jokes about women, people of color, or LGBTQ+ folks are brushed off as harmless, it teaches everyone that their pain just doesn’t count.
And it’s not just about old shows and movies, either. Even brand-new stories can fall into the same traps. Maybe there’s a blockbuster with a so-called “strong female character,” but she’s still mostly defined by the men she’s surrounded by. Or a popular song might hype up independence, but only within a pretty narrow set of boundaries. Sure, the surface changes, but the message underneath? It often stays the same.
Now, here’s the good news—pop culture can be a place for resistance, too. Sometimes, a new show or movie comes along and actually breaks the pattern. Suddenly, you’ve got real, complex characters and stories you’ve never seen before. Maybe a group of friends gets together to binge a series that centers on women’s experiences, or a film that tells the honest truth about racism. These moments matter, not just because they’re entertaining, but because they give us new ways to see the world—and ourselves.
And you know, it’s not about expecting every story to be perfect. What really counts is noticing the patterns, asking questions, and being open to letting go of stories that just don’t work anymore. When someone says, “That joke isn’t funny,” it’s not an attack—it’s actually an invitation to think a little differently.
Most of us don’t realize just how much pop culture shapes our beliefs. We think we’re just watching TV or listening to some music. But over time, all those stories add up. They become the background noise of daily life—the assumptions we don’t even notice we’re making.
But here’s the thing: you can always change the channel. You can look for stories that challenge old ideas, support creators who tell the truth, and be real about what needs to change. It’s not always comfortable, but it’s so necessary.
Pop culture feels powerful because it feels personal. The stories you love become part of who you are. And that’s why it matters so much. When the stories change, the world changes, too.
